The Bradley-Terry model

The Bradley-Terry model is a probability model for the outcome of paired comparisons. It assigns each item a positive strength parameter, and predicts that the probability of one item beating another depends only on the ratio of their strengths.

Given two items i and j with strength parameters p_i and p_j, the model states that the probability that i is preferred to j is the strength of i divided by the sum of the two strengths. Equivalently, writing the strengths as exponentials of real-valued scores, the probability is the softmax of the two scores.

The model is widely used in ranking problems where only pairwise outcomes are observed: chess and other games, consumer preference studies, and the reward modelling stage of reinforcement learning from human feedback, where a reward model is trained on pairs of responses that a human annotator ranked.

Fitting the model is usually done by maximum likelihood. The likelihood is concave in the log-strengths, so the optimum is unique up to an additive constant, which is fixed by a normalisation such as setting the strengths to sum to one.

A common criticism of the model is that it assumes transitivity: if i beats j and j beats k, it cannot represent a cyclic preference. Extensions relax this by allowing each item several strengths, one per context.
